equipment: Ultrasonic diffuser (typically 100-300 mL reservoir) for aromatic blends
Amber or cobalt glass dropper bottles (5-15 mL) for storing blends and diluted roll-ons
Digital scale reading to 0.1 g for salve making
Double boiler or a heatproof glass measuring cup set in a saucepan with a few inches of water
Mason jars with lids for infusing herbal oils
Fine-mesh strainer and cheesecloth for straining infused oils
Small metal tins or glass jars (30-60 mL / 1-2 oz) for finished salves
Labels and a permanent marker for naming, dating, and listing dilutions
Dedicated glass stirring rod or stainless spoon (stainless is fine here - no clay involved)
safety: Never apply undiluted essential oils to skin - Tisserand Institute calls this the single most common cause of adverse reactions; always dilute in a carrier oil, salve, or lotion.

Adult topical guideline: about 2% essential oil for body products (roughly 9 drops per 15 mL / 1 tablespoon of carrier, per the Tisserand/AromaWeb drop charts); use just 0.5-1% for facial products, children over 6, elderly users, and sensitive skin; AromaWeb recommends 1% for children and the elderly.

Respect oil-specific maximums from the Tisserand dilution chart: clove bud no more than 0.5%, holy basil up to 1%, and for phototoxicity lemon no more than 2% and grapefruit up to 4% in leave-on products (or avoid sun for 12-18 hours after applying phototoxic citrus).

Children: keep all essential-oil bottles locked away and never let children handle them - even two-year-olds have unscrewed caps and drunk the contents, causing emergency-room visits (Tisserand); follow the age-banded dilution chart, avoid essential oils entirely on babies under 3 months, and avoid menthol/1,8-cineole-rich oils (peppermint, eucalyptus) on or around young children.

Pets: diffuse only in ventilated spaces with the door open so animals can leave the room, never diffuse continuously around caged animals or birds, and be especially cautious with cats, which metabolize essential-oil constituents poorly (AromaWeb diffuser safety guidance).
Pregnancy, epilepsy, hypertension, and medication use all change which oils are safe - check a reputable safety reference (Tisserand, NAHA) or a qualified aromatherapist before use.
Do not take essential oils internally unless directed by a qualified practitioner (NAHA position).

If essential oil gets in an eye, wipe the closed lid with a cloth soaked in a fatty oil such as olive and/or flush with cool water (NAHA first aid); for skin reactions, wash with plain vegetable oil then soap and water - not just water.
Patch test every new blend or salve on the inner forearm and wait 24 hours before wider use.

phases.title: Phase 1 - Plan the dilution (all remedies)
steps: Decide who the remedy is for and choose the dilution ceiling before choosing oils: about 2% for a healthy adult body product, 1% for children over 6, elderly, or facially applied products, and 0.25-0.5% for ages 2-6 per Tisserand's age-banded chart.

Convert percent to drops with the standard chart math: at roughly 20 drops per mL, a 1% dilution is 4-5 drops per 15 mL (1 tablespoon) of carrier and a 2% dilution is about 9 drops per 15 mL - scale linearly for larger volumes.
Check each chosen oil against its individual dermal maximum (e.g., clove bud 0.5%) and phototoxicity limits (lemon 2%, grapefruit 4%) before finalizing the blend.
Write the recipe down - oil names, drop counts, carrier volume, and final percent - so the batch is reproducible and the label is honest.

phases.title: Phase 2 - Diffuser blends
steps: Fill the diffuser reservoir with clean tap or distilled water to its fill line (most home ultrasonic diffusers hold 100-300 mL).

Add 3-5 drops of essential oil per 100 mL of water as a starting point; AromaWeb's diffuser guidance is to begin with the low end (even 1-3 drops of a blend) and adjust, always deferring to the diffuser manufacturer's instructions.
Pre-mix multi-oil blends in a small amber bottle first (for example 2 parts lavender, 1 part sweet orange, 1 part cedarwood for a calming blend) so each session uses a consistent ratio.

Run the diffuser intermittently: 30-60 minutes on, then 30-60 minutes off; Robert Tisserand notes intermittent diffusion is both safer and MORE effective than continuous, because the nervous system habituates after about an hour.
Diffuse in a ventilated room, keep sessions shorter and doses lower when children, pregnant women, or pets share the space, and stop if anyone develops a headache or nausea.
Empty and wipe the reservoir between different blends so old oils do not accumulate in the unit.

phases.title: Phase 3 - Infuse the herbal oil (for salves)
steps: Slow (folk) method: fill a clean, dry mason jar one-quarter to one-half full of dried herbs (calendula, plantain, comfrey, lavender), cover completely with olive, sweet almond, or sunflower oil to near the top, cap, shake, and steep in a cool dark place for 4 to 6 weeks before straining (The Nerdy Farm Wife's preferred method).

Fast (heat) method: fill the jar one-third to one-half with dried herbs, cover with oil, set the uncapped jar down into a saucepan with a few inches of water, and warm on the lowest heat for 2 to 3 hours - if it starts to smell like deep-fried herbs it overheated and should be discarded.
Always use fully DRIED herbs - fresh plant material carries water that spoils the oil and invites botulism-friendly conditions.
Strain the finished oil through a fine-mesh strainer lined with cheesecloth, squeezing the herbs, and label the jar; carefully stored infused oils keep about a year.

phases.title: Phase 4 - Make the salve or balm
steps: Choose the beeswax-to-oil ratio from Humblebee & Me's tested ladder: 1 part beeswax to 5 parts oil by weight (about 17% beeswax) gives a classic soft salve that melts on skin contact, 1:4 (20%) gives a firmer salve, and 1:3 (25%) approaches a stiff balm/lotion-bar feel; The Nerdy Farm Wife's healing salve runs about 11-12% beeswax for an extra-soft texture.
For a standard 100 g batch, weigh 15-20 g beeswax pastilles and 80-85 g infused oil into a heatproof glass measuring cup.
Set the cup into a saucepan with a few inches of barely simmering water and heat gently just until the beeswax is completely melted, stirring occasionally.

Remove from heat and stir in essential oils at your planned dilution - e.g., about 1% for a general-purpose adult salve (The Nerdy Farm Wife's ~6 oz batch uses 15 drops tea tree plus 20 drops lavender, roughly 1%), plus an optional pinch (1/8 teaspoon) of rosemary antioxidant/ROE to lengthen shelf life.
Test the set by dropping a little on a cold spoon: too soft, melt back in a bit more beeswax; too hard, add a splash more oil.
Pour the warm liquid into clean tins or glass jars, cap after a skin forms, and leave undisturbed until fully cool and set before moving.

phases.title: Phase 5 - Label, store, and use
steps: Label every remedy with its contents, essential-oil dilution percent, date made, and who it is safe for (e.g., 'adults only' or 'kid-safe 1%').
Store salves and blend bottles in a cool, dark place; a well-made salve from fresh oils keeps about 1 year (rosemary antioxidant extends this), while infused oils alone keep about a year.
Use clean, dry fingers or a small spatula to scoop salve so water and microbes never enter the anhydrous product.
Apply salves to intact skin only - scrapes and dry patches, not deep wounds or broken, infected skin.
Discard any remedy that changes smell (crayon-like or rancid notes), color, or texture.

finishing: Salves and balms: cool completely before capping tightly; stored cool and dark they keep about 12 months, and rosemary antioxidant (ROE) or vitamin E slows rancidity.
Diffuser blend master bottles: store in amber glass with reducer caps, away from heat and sunlight; citrus-heavy blends are best used within 6-12 months.
Wipe diffusers dry after each use and deep-clean monthly per the manufacturer to prevent oil buildup and mold.
Keep every finished remedy, like every raw essential oil, in child-proof storage out of children's reach.
Record batch notes (recipe, date, texture verdict) so successful ratios can be repeated exactly.
tips: Master the cold-spoon test: it lets you fix a salve's texture while the pot is still warm instead of discovering a hockey puck after it sets.
Formulate at the LOWEST dilution that works - Tisserand's core principle is that dilution and risk are directly linked, and 1% is genuinely effective for everyday blends.
Calendula-infused olive oil is the most forgiving, all-purpose salve base for beginners and is gentle enough for most skin.
Pre-mixing a 'stock blend' of essential oils in one amber bottle keeps every diffuser session and salve batch consistent instead of re-counting drops from 4 bottles.
Intermittent diffusion (30-60 minutes on/off) is not just safer - Tisserand notes benefits do not increase with continuous running because the body habituates.
mistakes: Applying 'neat' (undiluted) essential oils to skin because a seller said it was safe - this is the top cause of sensitization, which can be lifelong.
Using adult dilutions or adult oils (peppermint, eucalyptus) on young children, or leaving bottles where a toddler can unscrew the cap.
Running a diffuser continuously all day in a closed room with pets or infants present instead of intermittently in ventilated space.
Infusing fresh (wet) herbs or letting water get into a salve - trapped moisture spoils the anhydrous product and can support dangerous bacteria.
Overheating the infusion or the beeswax melt on direct heat, which fries the herbs, degrades the oil, and shortens shelf life; always use a gentle water bath.
